extracted.intended_audience: press officers, public relations professionals, communications staff and scholars interested in media sourcing and press-release pickup
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate or craft press releases to maximize likelihood of media pickup by fitting them into reporters' routine sourcing channels, using Sigal's routine-channel theory. The rubric operationalizes sourcing channels and concrete release attributes that increase front-page pickup probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Official proceedings, press releases, press conferences, briefings, scheduled non-spontaneous events — the channel by which ~60% of front-page stories arrive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pickup-worthy release is one designed to slot into a routine channel a beat reporter already monitors. Emphasize calendar hooks, institutional forms, and placement where beats expect material (e.g., PR wires, beat inboxes, scheduled briefings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaks, off-the-record briefings, background sessions — informal ways reporters acquire news (about ~15% according to Sigal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A press release competes with informal channels by offering on-the-record specificity that a leak cannot. If aiming to displace informal sourcing, provide named, on-the-record authority and verifiable detail to reduce reporters' need to rely on leaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enterprise channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporter-initiated reporting: reporter's own observation, interviews initiated by the reporter, original research — accounting for roughly 25% of front-page material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pickup-worthy release lowers the cost-of-enterprise enough that the reporter chooses the routine path rather than pursuing original reporting; provide usable facts, ready-made quotes, documents, or access that reduce reporters' effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel-fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release land in a recognized channel (PR newswire, beat-reporter inbox, scheduled briefing, AP 'day book') rather than in a generic blast?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribute to the specific institutional channel reporters watch; avoid generic mass blasts. Placement determines visibility — even strong content can be invisible if sent through the wrong distribution path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official-source authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release foreground a titled official or institutional spokesperson whose authority a reporter can stake a story on? (Sigal: ~58% of Times/Post front-page sources were US officials.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use named officials with clear titles and institutional affiliation; institutional letterhead and clear attribution increase reporters' willingness to use the material as a primary source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine event scaffolding
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the release pegged to a calendared occasion (hearing, anniversary, scheduled report release, conference) so the reporter has a temporal hook?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie releases to known events or scheduled actions to provide reporters with a natural lead and editorial rationale for coverage. Calendar hooks make monitoring easier for beat reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of reportorial uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release pre-resolve the editor's 'is this real?' question via institutional letterhead, named author, peer-reviewed citation, embargoed copy of underlying document, etc.?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide verifiable supporting material (documents, citations, embargoed full reports) and clear provenance. The more a release reduces verification cost, the likelier pickup becomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the release distributed to the correct beat (health, business, courts, science) and pegged to that beat's evaluative criteria?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand what each beat values (timeliness, novelty, human impact, data) and craft the release and distribution so it matches the beat's routine expectations and criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureaucratic legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release come from an institution whose ongoing existence the beat already covers (e.g., NIH vs. an unknown advocacy group of the same scientific quality)? Pickup is higher for releases from long-covered institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage institutional standing and recognizable organizational identity; build or reference institutional relationships rather than relying solely on content quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-event vs. spontaneous event posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release transform a real event into a coverable one (preferred) rather than purely manufacture a pseudo-event staged only for coverage? Sigal (following Boorstin) notes staged 'pseudo-events' have different credibility dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to connect releases to substantive, verifiable occurrences rather than creating events solely for publicity; authenticity boosts long-run credibility with reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat-game posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release reflect a sustained, accurate sourcing relationship rather than a one-off attempt to crash the channel? Routine channels reward sources who don't burn reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain accuracy, reliability, and predictable behavior over time. One-off or unreliable senders are less likely to be monitored or trusted by beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable failure mode (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: A release from a non-recurring, non-official source pushed through a generic wire is often invisible because no beat has it on routine watch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid single-shot, generic-wire tactics from unknown senders. If you lack institutional standing or routine placement, either build relationships or craft the release to explicitly reduce verification and beat-alignment costs.
